questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of a circumvallate papilla taste bud, identify the apical structure indicated by pointer [ A ]:
options: Taste pore with microvilli
Basal reserve stem cell
Supporting sustentacular cell
Primary gustatory receptor
questions.explanation: The taste pore is the small apical mucosal opening through which microvilli of sensory gustatory cells project into the oral cavity to bind dissolved tastants.
questions.keyConcept: Taste pore: apical orifice transmitting tastants to sensory cell microvilli.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of the circumvallate taste bud, identify the elongated insulating cells indicated by pointer [ B ]:
options: Primary gustatory sensory cells
Supporting (sustentacular) cells
Basal undifferentiated stem cells
Antimicrobial secretory Paneth cells
questions.explanation: Supporting (sustentacular) cells span the entire height of the taste bud from the basal lamina to the taste pore, providing structural and metabolic insulation for gustatory receptor cells.
questions.keyConcept: Sustentacular cells: full-height supportive cells insulating sensory receptors.

questions.text: Examine this high-yield H&E histological section of a major salivary gland. Which defining histological feature confirms that this specimen is the parotid gland?
options: Predominantly mucous tubules capped with serous demilunes
Purely mucous acini with flattened basal peripheral nuclei
Purely serous acini with narrow lumens and intercalated ducts
Co-dominant mixture of discrete serous and mucous acini
questions.explanation: The human parotid gland is 100% serous, exhibiting round basophilic acini with narrow lumens, spherical central nuclei, apical zymogen granules, and absence of mucous tubules.
questions.keyConcept: Parotid = purely serous acini with round central nuclei and intercalated ducts.

questions.text: Examine this H&E cross-section of the gastrointestinal tract. What definitive landmark restricts the anatomical diagnosis to the duodenum?
options: Aggregated Peyer lymphoid patches in the lamina propria and submucosa
Complete absence of mucosal villi with long straight vertical crypts
Stratified squamous non-keratinized mucosal epithelial lining
Branched coiled Brunner glands packed within the submucosal layer
questions.explanation: Brunner (duodenal) glands are branched coiled tubular mucous glands confined specifically to the submucosa of the duodenum, secreting alkaline mucin (pH 8.1–9.3) to protect against gastric acid.
questions.keyConcept: Submucosal Brunner glands are exclusively found in the duodenum.

questions.text: This transmission electron micrograph (TEM) demonstrates pyramidal cells at the base of the crypts of Lieberkühn with prominent apical dense granules. What is their primary function?
options: Absorption of dietary lipids and synthesis of core chylomicrons
Secretion of antimicrobial alpha-defensins and lysozyme enzymes
Secretion of lubricating mucin glycoproteins by exocytosis
Systemic release of endocrine peptides gastrin and cholecystokinin
questions.explanation: Paneth cells occupy the bases of small intestinal crypts and contain large apical eosinophilic secretory granules containing lysozyme, phospholipase A2, and alpha-defensins providing mucosal immunity.
questions.keyConcept: Paneth cells secrete antimicrobial defensins and lysozyme at intestinal crypt bases.

questions.text: Examine this cross-section of the vermiform appendix. Which histological characteristic most definitively distinguishes the appendix from the colon?
options: Prominent outer taeniae coli formed by discrete longitudinal muscle bands
Numerous tall slender mucosal villi lined by microvillar enterocytes
Confluent lymphoid follicles infiltrating the lamina propria and submucosa
Complete absence of straight tubular crypts of Lieberkühn
questions.explanation: The vermiform appendix possesses a complete outer longitudinal muscle coat (no taeniae coli) and massive, confluent lymphoid follicles with germinal centers effacing the lamina propria and submucosa.
questions.keyConcept: Appendix: circular continuous longitudinal coat + dense circumferential lymphoid ring.

questions.text: This endoscopic biopsy from the distal esophagus of a patient with chronic reflux demonstrates epithelial replacement. What is the pathognomonic diagnostic finding?
options: Columnar intestinal metaplasia containing alcian blue-positive goblet cells
Severe squamous cell dysplasia with intact underlying basal membrane
Eosinophilic microabscesses without glandular or goblet cell conversion
Dense submucosal lymphoid follicles with reactive germinal centers
questions.explanation: Barrett esophagus is defined histologically by intestinal metaplasia where normal squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar cells containing true goblet cells, conferring risk for adenocarcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Barrett esophagus: intestinal metaplasia with true goblet cells above GE junction.

questions.text: Examine this section from a benign parotid neoplasm (pleomorphic adenoma). What dual histological components define this mixed tumor?
options: Bilayered oncocytic columnar cells overlying dense lymphoid stroma
Solid sheets of poorly differentiated clear cells with vascular invasion
Sheets of mature signet ring cells filled with abundant intracellular mucin
Epithelial ductal structures embedded in myxoid and chondroid stroma
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma (mixed tumor) displays epithelial ductal structures and sheets intermingled with myxoid, chondroid, or fibrous mesenchymal-like stroma elaborated by neoplastic myoepithelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Pleomorphic adenoma = epithelial ducts embedded in myxochondroid matrix.

questions.text: This photomicrograph demonstrates Warthin tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum). What microscopic architecture establishes the diagnosis?
options: Malignant stratified squamous islands surrounded by marked desmoplasia
Acellular laminated chitinous membranes with calcified brood capsules
Bilayered oncocytic epithelium lining cysts over lymphoid stroma with follicles
Mucin-secreting signet ring cells infiltrating the parotid gland capsule
questions.explanation: Warthin tumor consists of cystic spaces with papillary foldings lined by a uniform double layer of pink oncocytic columnar cells resting upon a dense lymphoid stroma with germinal centers.
questions.keyConcept: Warthin tumor: bilayered oncocytic epithelium + lymphoid stroma with germinal centers.

questions.text: This liver biopsy stained with Masson trichrome demonstrates blue-staining fibrous bands. What pathological triad defines liver cirrhosis?
options: Diffuse bridging fibrosis, architectural disruption, and regenerative nodules
Focal portal triaditis, central vein thrombosis, and preserved liver plates
Centrilobular macrovesicular steatosis without significant fibrous septation
Non-caseating granulomas with complete preservation of lobular architecture
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis is defined pathologically by diffuse bridging fibrosis (blue on Masson trichrome), complete loss of normal lobular architecture, and parenchymal nodular regeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Cirrhosis triad: diffuse fibrosis + regenerative nodules + architectural disruption.

questions.text: A patient with cirrhosis develops a liver mass showing malignant hepatocytes. Which histological feature confirms hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)?
options: Orderly single-cell thick cords bordered by normal sinusoidal endothelial cells
Malignant glandular tubules producing abundant intracytoplasmic mucin
Small uniform round blue neuroendocrine cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin
Markedly thickened liver cell trabeculae (>3 cells thick) with atypical mitoses
questions.explanation: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by loss of reticulin framework, markedly thickened trabeculae (>3 cells thick), pseudoacinar architecture, pleomorphic nuclei, and atypical mitoses.
questions.keyConcept: HCC: thick trabeculae (>3 cells), nuclear atypia, and loss of reticulin network.

questions.text: Examine this hepatic bilharziasis specimen (Symmers clay-pipe-stem fibrosis). What distinguishes schistosomal hepatic fibrosis from true cirrhosis?
options: Widespread hepatocellular necrosis with diffuse micro-nodular regeneration
Preservation of normal lobular architecture and absence of regenerative nodules
Severe diffuse macrovesicular fatty change affecting all lobular zones
Primary obliteration of major hepatic veins with centrilobular congestion
questions.explanation: In Symmers clay-pipe-stem fibrosis, granulomatous and dense fibrosis is restricted to periportal spaces, while lobular architecture and central veins are preserved without regenerative nodules.
questions.keyConcept: Symmers fibrosis: periportal fibrosis with preserved lobular architecture (non-cirrhotic).

title: Practical — Parasitology
subtitle: GIT Parasites, Eggs, Adults & Snail Vectors

questions.text: Identify this parasite egg recovered from the stool of a patient with dysentery. What morphological feature definitively identifies Schistosoma mansoni?
options: Small oval yellowish-brown operculated shell containing a ciliated miracidium
Spherical thick-shelled brown egg bearing a conspicuous terminal spine
Barrel-shaped golden egg with translucent protruding bipolar mucoid plugs
Large elongated oval translucent shell bearing a prominent sharp lateral spine
questions.explanation: Schistosoma mansoni eggs measure 114–180 µm by 45–70 µm and feature a prominent sharp lateral spine near the posterior pole, in contrast to S. haematobium (terminal spine).
questions.keyConcept: Schistosoma mansoni egg = prominent sharp lateral spine.

questions.text: Identify this adult liver fluke recovered from a biliary tract prosection. Which feature differentiates Fasciola gigantica from Fasciola hepatica?
options: Presence of a third specialized genital sucker (gonotyl) around genital pore
Complete absence of anterior oral and ventral fixation acetabula
Elongated body (up to 7.5 cm) with nearly parallel margins and faint shoulders
Unbranched simple tubular intestinal ceca extending to the posterior tip
questions.explanation: Fasciola gigantica is significantly longer (25–75 mm) than F. hepatica (20–30 mm), possesses nearly parallel lateral margins, and displays a less prominent cephalic cone and indistinct shoulders.
questions.keyConcept: Fasciola gigantica: large size (up to 7.5 cm), parallel borders, faint shoulders.

questions.text: Identify this freshwater snail shell collected from Egyptian water channels. What morphological criteria confirm Biomphalaria alexandrina?
options: Dextral conical shell with a sharp pointed apex and very large body whorl
Sinistral, discoidal shell coiled horizontally like a disk with aperture to left
Tall turreted spiral shell with an elongated narrow aperture on the right
Globular thick operculated shell with prominent concentric exterior ridges
questions.explanation: Biomphalaria alexandrina is the intermediate snail host of Schistosoma mansoni in Egypt; its shell is planorboid (discoidal, flat whorls) and sinistral (aperture opens to the left).
questions.keyConcept: Biomphalaria alexandrina: discoidal, sinistral shell; vector for S. mansoni.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of a hepatic hydatid cyst (Echinococcus granulosus). Identify the distinctive acellular parasite layer:
options: Acellular, chitinous laminated (cuticular) membrane with fine striations
Inner nucleated germinal layer actively generating scolices and brood capsules
Dense outer vascularized fibrous pseudocapsule synthesized by the host liver
Calcified calcareous corpuscle layer lining the internal cyst cavity
questions.explanation: The hydatid cyst wall consists of an outer acellular laminated cuticular membrane (secreted by the parasite, appearing hyaline and striated) and an inner cellular germinal layer that buds brood capsules.
questions.keyConcept: Hydatid wall: outer acellular laminated layer + inner nucleated germinal layer.

questions.text: Identify this parasite egg collected by perianal Scotch tape swab in a child with nocturnal pruritus ani:
options: Planoconvex D-shaped transparent egg of Enterobius vermicularis
Thick-shelled corticated egg of Ascaris lumbricoides with wavy coat
Thin-shelled oval egg of Ancylostoma duodenale with clear space
Lemon-shaped egg of Trichuris trichiura with two polar plugs
questions.explanation: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) eggs are colorless, translucent, 50–60 µm long, and characteristically planoconvex (D-shaped, flattened on one side and convex on the other).
questions.keyConcept: Enterobius vermicularis egg: planoconvex (D-shaped), colorless, transparent shell.

questions.text: Identify this parasite egg found in a stool wet mount from an anemic patient. What morphological hallmark identifies Trichuris trichiura?
options: Yellow operculated oval shell with an abopercular thickening and miracidium
Spherical brown egg with a thick radially striated embryophore and hooklets
Golden-brown barrel-shaped shell with prominent transparent bipolar mucoid plugs
Ovoid thin-shelled transparent egg containing an unsegmented granular ovum
questions.explanation: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) eggs are barrel-shaped (50–54 µm by 22 µm), golden-brown, with a thick smooth shell and two characteristic translucent mucoid plugs protruding from both poles.
questions.keyConcept: Trichuris trichiura egg: barrel-shaped with bipolar mucoid plugs.

questions.text: In a cadaveric prosection of the celiac trunk at the level of T12, which of the following is an immediate primary branch of the trunk?
options: Gastroduodenal artery arising behind the first part of the duodenum
Splenic artery coursing tortuously along the upper border of pancreas
Right gastric artery running along the lesser curvature of stomach
Superior mesenteric artery descending anterior to the third part of duodenum
questions.explanation: The celiac trunk trifurcates into the left gastric artery, splenic artery (running along the upper pancreatic border to the spleen), and common hepatic artery.
questions.keyConcept: Celiac trunk trifurcation: Left gastric, Splenic, and Common hepatic arteries.

questions.text: During dissection of the inguinal canal, identify the structure that reinforces the posterior wall in its medial third:
options: Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle with its intercrural fibers
Curved shelving border of the inguinal ligament (Poupart ligament)
Reflected triangular pectineal ligament (Cooper ligament) on pecten pubis
Conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) behind the superficial inguinal ring
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed in its lateral two-thirds by the fascia transversalis and in its medial third by the conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) formed by internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
questions.keyConcept: Inguinal canal posterior wall: Fascia transversalis (lateral) + Conjoint tendon (medial).

questions.text: At the porta hepatis (free margin of the lesser omentum), what is the correct spatial arrangement of the structures from anterior to posterior?
options: Portal vein (anterior), Hepatic artery proper (middle), Bile duct (posterior)
Bile duct (anterior-right), Hepatic artery proper (anterior-left), Portal vein (posterior)
Hepatic artery proper (anterior), Portal vein (middle), Bile duct (posterior)
Inferior vena cava (anterior), Bile duct (middle), Hepatic artery (posterior)
questions.explanation: In the free edge of the lesser omentum: the common bile duct lies anterolaterally to the right, the hepatic artery proper lies anteromedially to the left, and the portal vein lies posteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Porta hepatis relation: Duct on Right, Artery on Left, Portal Vein Behind.

questions.text: Esophageal manometry in a 35-year-old with dysphagia reveals unrelaxed LES and aperistalsis (achalasia). What is the primary neurogenic defect?
options: Degeneration of inhibitory myenteric neurons producing nitric oxide and VIP
Excessive cholinergic vagal outflow hyperpolarizing esophageal smooth muscle
Loss of sensory afferent fibers in the submucosal Meissner nerve plexus
Autoimmune destruction of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at striated endplates
questions.explanation: Achalasia results from selective degeneration of postganglionic inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus that release nitric oxide (NO) and VIP, preventing lower esophageal sphincter relaxation.
questions.keyConcept: Achalasia: loss of NO/VIP inhibitory myenteric neurons causes aperistalsis and unrelaxed LES.

questions.text: In a lab experiment, introducing acidic chyme (pH < 4.5) into the duodenum triggers copious watery pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate. Which hormone mediates this response?
options: Cholecystokinin (CCK), secreted by mucosal I-cells in response to peptides
Gastrin, released from gastric antral G-cells in response to distension
Motilin, released from upper intestinal M-cells during interdigestive migrating complexes
Secretin, secreted by mucosal S-cells in response to intraluminal hydrogen ions
questions.explanation: Secretin is released by duodenal S-cells when luminal pH drops below 4.5. It acts on pancreatic ductular cells via cAMP to stimulate secretion of large volumes of watery, bicarbonate-rich juice.
questions.keyConcept: Secretin: triggered by duodenal acid -> stimulates ductal aqueous HCO3- secretion.

questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with hepatosplenomegaly, tremor, and Kayser-Fleischer rings (Wilson disease). What is the pathognomonic serum and urine biochemical profile?
options: Elevated serum ceruloplasmin with markedly decreased urinary copper clearance
Markedly elevated serum ferritin, high transferrin saturation, and normal copper
Decreased serum ceruloplasmin, increased free serum copper, and elevated 24-hour urine copper
Deficiency of alpha-1 antitrypsin with normal serum ceruloplasmin and urinary copper
questions.explanation: Wilson disease (ATP7B mutation) causes impaired copper incorporation into apoceruloplasmin (low ceruloplasmin) and blocked biliary excretion, causing high free serum copper and high urinary copper excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Wilson disease: low serum ceruloplasmin + high urinary copper excretion (ATP7B defect).

questions.text: A 52-year-old female presents with painless jaundice and clay-colored stools. Labs: Total Bilirubin 12 mg/dL, Direct Bilirubin 9.5 mg/dL, and marked elevation of ALP and GGT with mild ALT/AST elevation. What is the diagnosis?
options: Acute viral hepatocellular hepatitis with diffuse hepatic cytolysis
Pre-hepatic hemolytic anemia with predominant unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
Post-hepatic (obstructive/cholestatic) jaundice
Gilbert syndrome caused by reduced promoter activity of glucuronyl transferase
questions.explanation: Obstructive cholestatic jaundice shows predominant conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia with disproportionate elevation of biliary canalicular enzymes (ALP and GGT) and clay stools from lack of stercobilin.
questions.keyConcept: Cholestatic jaundice: high direct bilirubin + marked elevation of ALP and GGT.

title: Practical — Microbiology
subtitle: Stool Culture, Selective Media & Enteric Pathogens

questions.text: A stool culture on MacConkey agar shows pale non-lactose-fermenting colonies. Subculture on Salmonella-Shigella (SS) agar produces colonies with black centers. Identify the pathogen:
options: Shigella dysenteriae (non-lactose fermenter producing colorless colonies without H2S)
Salmonella enterica (H2S production creates black iron sulfide precipitate)
Escherichia coli (vigorous lactose fermenter producing bright pink dry colonies)
Vibrio cholerae (sucrose fermenter producing bright yellow colonies on TCBS agar)
questions.explanation: On MacConkey agar, Salmonella and Shigella are pale (non-lactose fermenters). On SS agar, Salmonella produces H2S gas which reacts with ferric citrate to produce black-centered colonies.
questions.keyConcept: Salmonella on SS agar = non-lactose fermenting colonies with black H2S centers.

questions.text: Stool from a patient with rice-water diarrhea is cultured on Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile Salts-Sucrose (TCBS) agar, yielding bright yellow colonies. Microscopic examination shows curved Gram-negative rods with darting motility. What is the organism?
options: Vibrio cholerae (sucrose fermentation lowers pH and turns bromothymol blue yellow)
Campylobacter jejuni (microaerophilic thermophilic curved rod growing on Skirrow agar)
Helicobacter pylori (potent urease-producing curved rod colonizing gastric antrum)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa (non-fermenting Gram-negative rod producing green pyocyanin pigment)
questions.explanation: TCBS agar is highly selective and differential for Vibrio. Vibrio cholerae ferments sucrose, producing acid that turns the bromothymol blue pH indicator yellow.
questions.keyConcept: Vibrio cholerae: yellow colonies on TCBS agar + curved Gram-negative rods.

subjects.name: Clinical
lectureNames: Peptic Ulcer Endoscopy & H. pylori Therapy

questions.text: A 45-year-old smoker taking NSAIDs presents with burning epigastric pain 2–3 hours after meals relieved by food. Endoscopy reveals a punched-out duodenal ulcer. What is the essential medical management?
options: Emergency partial gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy reconstruction
High-dose continuous NSAID therapy combined with oral misoprostol monotherapy
Long-term empiric belladonna alkaloid therapy to suppress vagal gastric motility
Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) along with testing and eradication therapy for Helicobacter pylori
questions.explanation: Duodenal ulcers typically cause pain relieved by food and nocturnal pain. Treatment requires profound acid suppression with a PPI and eradication of H. pylori (triple or quadruple regimen).
questions.keyConcept: Duodenal ulcer: epigastric pain relieved by food; treat with PPI + H. pylori eradication.

questions.text: A patient with cirrhosis presents with ascites, splenomegaly, and dilated tortuous superficial periumbilical veins radiating outward (caput medusae). What portosystemic collateral channel produces this sign?
options: Superior vena cava collaterals anastomosing with internal mammary vessels
Left gastric veins anastomosing with lower esophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
Superior rectal vein anastomosing with middle and inferior rectal branches of internal iliac
Recanalized paraumbilical veins communicating with systemic epigastric veins
questions.explanation: Caput medusae results from severe portal hypertension where portal venous blood is shunted through recanalized paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament into superficial and inferior epigastric veins.
questions.keyConcept: Caput medusae = portosystemic shunt through recanalized paraumbilical veins.
